claims.text: The untreated material is an as-deposited, single-phase, equiatomic NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy with a nanocrystalline columnar BCC microstructure.
Approximately 20 at.% Re is incorporated to form Nb20Mo20Ta20W20Re20.
The Re-modified alloy can retain a single-phase BCC structure under the specified sputtering conditions.
Re addition will refine the grain size.
Re addition will increase grain-boundary density.
Re addition will increase lattice distortion and excess free volume.
Re addition will produce several-nanometer-wide amorphous intergranular films.
Grain refinement and amorphous grain-boundary films will facilitate dislocation motion.
The modified boundaries will mitigate grain-boundary embrittlement.
The refined microstructure and amorphous boundary films will act as irradiation-defect sinks.
The proposed defect-sink structure will suppress helium-bubble coalescence.
Relative to Re-free NbMoTaW, NbMoTaWRe will have greater room-temperature strain to failure and plastic deformation.
Adding Re will not significantly reduce mechanical strength at 1600 °C.
The amorphous boundary films will preserve high-temperature performance because they do not compromise the alloy's inherent BCC strength.
Adding Re will maintain irradiation resistance under 120 keV He2+ implantation at a fluence of 1 × 10^16 ions/cm² and a dose rate of approximately 1 × 10^13 ions/cm²/s.
The Re-containing alloy will show less helium-bubble agglomeration than Re-free NbMoTaW.
The Re-containing alloy will show less irradiation-induced hardening than Re-free NbMoTaW.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has excellent high-temperature strength but very poor room-temperature ductility.
Prior observations in similar systems support ductility improvement through Re-induced grain refinement and amorphous boundary formation.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires maintenance of a single-phase BCC structure, while the mediator predicts several-nanometer-wide amorphous intergranular material. A BCC matrix containing a distinct amorphous grain-boundary phase is not strictly single-phase unless the films are being classified as interfacial complexions rather than a separate phase.

The central claim only requires irradiation resistance to be maintained, but the falsification rule rejects similar helium-bubble segregation or hardening and thus effectively requires irradiation performance to improve rather than merely remain non-degraded.
